lead: Every file, every page of memory and every device in a computer is shared by many processes, and some of those uses must be stopped. Protection is the part of the kernel that answers one question for every access: may this subject use this object in this way? It compares the request with the rights the process holds, then allows or denies it. The same check protects an exam cell's results file, a bank's ledger on a shared server, and your UPI app's data on a phone where other apps also run.
prereq: You need Unit 1 on dual mode operation and the role of the kernel, and Unit 5 on file attributes and access methods.

blocks.text: A subject is the active thing that asks for something, normally a process acting for a user. An object is anything the kernel can name and hand out: a file, a page of memory, a printer, a network socket. A right (also called a permission or an access right) is one permitted way of using that object: read, write, execute, append, delete. Protection is the mechanism that binds the three together.

Protection exists for three goals. Controlled access: a process touches only the objects it is allowed to touch, and only in allowed ways. Detection of programming errors: a bug that would write past the end of an array into another program's memory is stopped at the moment of the write, instead of silently corrupting data. Prevention of misuse of rights: a user who may read a file cannot quietly pass that right on, and cannot use a right for a purpose it was never meant for.
Protection is wider than files. It covers memory segments, CPU time, devices, and the message queues two processes share. Files are only the easiest place to see it.

items: The process issues a request: a system call naming an object and a mode, such as open("results.dat", "r").
The kernel's reference monitor looks up the domain of the process, which is the set of rights it holds at this moment (see 6.2).
If the domain contains read on results.dat, the access proceeds. If not, the call fails with an error (EACCES in Linux) and the object is not touched.

blocks.text: Protection and security are not the same word. Protection is internal and mechanical: the kernel decides each access from stored rights, and the decision can be read off the code. Security is trust against a deliberate attacker: whether the mechanism, the people who hold the passwords, and the network around the machine can keep an intruder out.

A file with mode 600 is protected: only its owner may read or write it. If the owner's password is 1234, the file is still not secure. The protection decision is right; the assumption behind it is false.

So protection is a mechanism, and security is the property you hope the whole system has. Security needs protection plus authentication, patching, physical locks and audit (see 6.6). The check itself behaves the same whether the request is honest or hostile, which is why one reference monitor serves both.
These seven principles are the classic design rules for protection systems. Some syllabi call them the design principles of protection.

items: Least privilege. Give each process the smallest set of rights that lets it finish its job, and take them back when it finishes. The exam cell program below needs read on one file and append on another, nothing more.

Need-to-know. Give a process access only to information it has a reason to use. This is the data version of least privilege: that same program has no business reading other sections' mark files even for a moment.
Fail-safe defaults. The default answer is deny; access is granted explicitly. A newly created file is readable by its owner only, not by everyone, until the owner widens it.
Separation of privilege. Require two independent conditions rather than one. A transfer above a set limit needs the operator's approval and the manager's, so one stolen password is not enough.

Economy of mechanism. Keep the checking code small and simple, because every extra line is a place where a check can be skipped. One reference monitor that all calls pass through beats checks scattered across the kernel.

Least common mechanism. Share as little state between users as possible, because shared state is a channel between them. Give each user a private temporary directory instead of one world-writable /tmp.

Separation of policy from mechanism. The mechanism is the check; the policy is the rule it enforces. Changing "interns may not read salary files" should mean editing an access list, not rewriting kernel code.

figure.caption: One access request, one decision: the reference monitor compares the request with the rights in the process's domain and either lets it through or returns an error. Notice that the process never reaches the file without passing the check.

spec.title: One access, one decision
spec.aria: A process issues a request on a file, the reference monitor compares it with the rights in the process domain, and the request is either allowed or denied.

examples.question: An exam cell runs a program called check_marks. Its directory holds 12 files: results.dat, audit.log, and 10 mark files belonging to other sections. The program must only read results.dat and append to audit.log. (a) Write its rights under least privilege and count them. (b) A programmer instead grants read and write on all 12 files. Count the rights granted and the excess over the needed set. (c) Name the two principles that (b) breaks.
steps: Needed set: read on results.dat is 1 right; append on audit.log is 1 right. Total under least privilege = 2 rights.
Append and not write on audit.log: write would also allow overwriting earlier entries, so append is the smallest right that does the job.
Wide grant: 2 rights (read and write) on each of 12 files, so 2 × 12 = 24 rights.
Excess over the needed set = 24 − 2 = 22 rights the program never uses.
(b) breaks least privilege, because write on files it never writes is more than it needs, and need-to-know, because it can now read the 10 mark files of other sections.
examples.answer: Least privilege gives 2 rights; the wide grant gives 24 rights, which is 22 more than needed.
examples.check:
files = 12
rights_per_file = 2
needed = 1 + 1
wide = files * rights_per_file
excess = wide - needed
print(needed)
print(wide)
print(excess)

traps: Protection and security are not the same. Protection is the kernel's internal check; security is whether that check, the people and the network can be trusted. A comparison question needs both halves.
Protection is not only about files. Memory, CPU time, devices and inter-process messages are objects too, and a question about 'objects' expects you to list them.
Least privilege and need-to-know look alike but answer different questions: how much a process may do (rights) versus how much it may know (information).
Fail-safe defaults means deny until something is allowed, not allow until something goes wrong. A new file readable by everyone is the classic wrong answer.

quiz.q: Define subject, object and right, with one example of each.
quiz.a: Subject: the active requester, such as the process running the exam cell program. Object: a resource the kernel names, such as the file results.dat. Right: one permitted use of an object, such as read on results.dat.

quiz.q: State the three goals of protection.
quiz.a: Controlled access to objects; detection of programming errors such as an out-of-range write; prevention of misuse of rights, including passing a right on without permission.

quiz.q: Distinguish protection from security in one sentence, with an example.
quiz.a: Protection is the kernel's internal check of each access; security is whether the whole system can be trusted against a deliberate attacker. A file with mode 600 is protected, but if the owner's password is 1234 it is not secure.

quiz.q: A directory holds 8 files. A program needs only read on a.dat and write on b.dat, both inside that directory. Count its rights under least privilege, then under a grant of read and write on every file, then the excess.
quiz.a: Least privilege: 1 + 1 = 2 rights. Wide grant: 8 files × 2 rights = 16 rights. Excess: 16 − 2 = 14 rights.

quiz.q: Why does economy of mechanism reduce the chance of a protection failure?
quiz.a: Every line of checking code is a place where a condition can be missed or a path can slip past the check. A small reference monitor that every access must pass is easier to review and test than checks scattered through a large kernel, so fewer bypasses survive.

quiz.q: Two programs must both add records to one audit log. Which principle is at risk, and what design keeps it?
quiz.a: Least common mechanism: the shared log is state shared between two users, so one program can read or overwrite the other's entries. The fix is a small logging service that only appends, with each program holding append rights on the log and no read right.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same principles scale far beyond one kernel: cloud identity policies are written as least-privilege rules, SELinux and AppArmor add system-wide mandatory rules on top of the permissive ones, and verified microkernels push economy of mechanism to its limit by keeping the trusted code tiny. Search for the reference monitor concept, mandatory versus discretionary access control, and the Bell–LaPadula model as the next step after this unit.
